sec.title: Background
sec.p: Observational studies and small randomized controlled trials have suggested the benefits of early introduction of sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) in acute heart failure (AHF). However, current evidence on their efficacy and safety in this clinical setting remains limited.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We performed a systematic review and meta‐analysis to assess efficacy/safety of early use of SGLT2is in AHF. PUBMED/EMBASE/Cochrane were searched from inception to May 31, 2024, for randomized controlled trials evaluating outcomes of SGLT2i early initiation in patients with AHF. Efficacy outcomes were all‐cause death and heart failure rehospitalizations. Safety outcomes included acute kidney injury, ketoacidosis, urinary tract infections, hypotension, and hypoglycemia. Early initiation was defined as performed before or shortly after discharge (within 3 days). A sensitivity analysis was conducted, including only patients with initiation before discharge.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Seven randomized controlled trials that enrolled 2320 patients were included. Early use of SGLT2is was associated with a significant reduction in all‐cause death (odds ratio, 0.71 [95% CI, 0.55–0.92; 95% PI, 0.55–0.98]) and HF rehospitalizations (odds ratio, 0.73 [95% CI, 0.57–0.94; 95% PI, 0.58–0.93]), even after adjusting for follow‐up duration. SGLT2i initiation before discharge yielded consistent results for efficacy outcomes. Safety outcomes could not be usefully determined because of a low events rate resulting in wide CIs. The impact of diabetic status remains basically unknown due to the small number of available randomized controlled trials investigating this population.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Early introduction of SGLT2is in AHF improves all‐cause death and rehospitalization rates, can be performed before discharge, and should be offered to most patients with AHF.

list-item.p: Early introduction of sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors in settings of acute heart failure improves all‐cause death and rehospitalization rates.
Early introduction of sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors in acute heart failure can be performed before discharge and should be offered to most patients with acute heart failure.

body.p: Acute heart failure (AHF) refers to rapid or gradual onset of symptoms or signs of heart failure (HF), severe enough to lead to an unplanned visit or intravenous treatment but, above all, hospital admission or an emergency department visit. 1 Despite recent advances, AHF remains a leading global cause of hospitalizations and death and hence heavy organizational and financial burden on health care systems. Importantly, this burden is expected to grow 2 and has already had a strong negative impact on patients themselves, with an in‐hospital mortality rate from 5% to 10%, and postdischarge 1‐year mortality rate of 25% to 30%, 3 , 4 urging improvement of specific management.

In this perspective, the recent surge of sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) represented a major advancement, demonstrating unique efficacy across the whole spectrum of chronic HF in reducing recurrent hospitalizations and cardiovascular death, 5 resulting in a class I recommendation for the baseline treatment of all patients with HF in both the 2022 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association/Heart Failure Society of America guidelines and the 2023 update of the 2021 European guidelines, regardless of left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) or the presence of diabetes. 1 , 6 , 7 In settings of AHF, many novel specific treatments have been attempted without yielding significant improvements and showing even by contrast disappointing results on the mortality rate. 8 , 9 Until recently, AHF usual initial management primarily consists of diuretic therapy and addressing specific triggers, while simultaneously initiating and uptitrating guideline‐directed medical therapy (GDMT) as soon as possible. 1 , 6 , 7

Given the promising results of SGLT2is in chronic HF, several randomized controlled trials have sought to evaluate their relevance in AHF, demonstrating consistent efficacy in decongestion, albeit with limited evidence for survival improvement, 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 and persistent concerns about the occurrence of adverse events such as acute kidney injury (AKI), ketoacidosis, or urinary tract infections, representing potential limitations to their early introduction, as highlighted in both American and European guidelines. 1 , 6 , 7 , 17 However, many of these studies were not powered to study impactful end points such as all‐cause death or rehospitalization rates and may be subject to biases due to the small scale of patient populations or the limited number of participating centers.
Therefore, we conducted a pooled data meta‐analysis to assess the efficacy and safety of early initiation of SGLT2i add‐on therapy in patients hospitalized for AHF.

sec.title: Data Access and Responsibility
sec.p: The authors declare that all supporting data are available within the article and its online supplementary files.

sec.title: Search Strategy
sec.p: Databases (PUBMED, EMBASE, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials) were searched, without language restriction, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing SGLT2i add‐on therapy in settings of AHF, using the search terms as outlined in Table S1, from inception to May 31, 2024. The search was kept current by setting up automated reminders from PUBMED for new publications. Institutional review committee approval was not required given that this is a meta‐analysis of published data. The study was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD42024556171).

sec.title: Article Selection
sec.p: Titles and abstracts of studies retrieved using the search strategy were independently screened by 2 investigators (C.D. and M.C.) to identify randomized controlled clinical trials with an active arm involving the initiation of an SGLT2i (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, sotagliflozin) in patients hospitalized with AHF. RCTs including patients with stable and chronic HF without acute exacerbation requiring unplanned hospitalization were not included. No minimum sample size was required for inclusion. The full texts of potentially eligible studies were retrieved and independently assessed for eligibility by the 2 investigators. Discrepancies between investigators were discussed collegially, and the final decision was then made by consensus.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: Efficacy outcomes of interest were all‐cause death (primary end point), HF rehospitalizations, and the composite of cardiovascular death or HF events (encompassing urgent visits and unplanned hospitalizations for AHF). Safety outcomes included the occurrence of AKI, ketoacidosis, urinary tract infections, hypotension, and hypoglycemia. The definitions of each event used by each trial were used in this analysis. The events reported at the longest follow‐up time point were abstracted from each of the trials.

sec.title: Risk‐of‐Bias Assessment
sec.p: Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool for RCTs, 18 which separates 5 fixed sets of domains of bias: (1) bias from the randomization process, (2) bias due to deviations from intended interventions, (3) bias due to missing outcome data, (4) bias in the measurement of the outcome, and (5) bias in the selection of reported results (each of them graded as “low,” “high,” or “some concerns”). Assessment for publication bias was limited due to the small number of RCTs included (<10), especially for funnel plot and Egger's test. 19

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: The meta‐analysis was performed in line with recommendations from the Cochrane Collaboration and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses Statement (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses checklist provided in Table S2), 20 , 21 using R software version 4.3.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) and the R packages meta and metafor. All the efficacy and safety outcomes studied were dichotomous. Hence, the number of events and total sample size in each group were extracted from each study for each outcome of interest. A pooled analysis was then conducted by aggregating the data to calculate the odds ratios (ORs) and corresponding 95% CIs for each dichotomous outcome. Initially, the DerSimonian and Laird random‐effects model was used because, on the basis of preexisting clinical and pathophysiological considerations, 1 , 6 , 7 , 17 we could not rule out the possibility that the observed estimates of treatment effect might vary across studies because of real differences in the treatment effect in each study as well as sampling variability. 20 , 22 Statistical heterogeneity was initially assessed using the I 2 statistic, which represents the proportion of total variation observed between trials that is attributable to differences between trials rather than sampling error (chance), with I 2 ≥50% considered indicative of substantial heterogeneity. 20 However, because the I 2 statistic does not tell us how much the effect size varies between studies, 23 we further assessed between‐study heterogeneity by presenting (1) an estimate of the between‐study variance (τ2), which reflects the variability in intervention effects across studies 20 ; and (2) the 95% prediction interval (PI), when ≥3 studies were available, representing the potential range of true effect sizes in a hypothetical future study that is similar to those included in the meta‐analysis, providing a more comprehensive estimate of the variability in treatment effects. 20 , 24

sec.title: Sensitivity Analysis
sec.p: Due to the risk of poor‐quality estimates with the random‐effects model in cases of few studies or when studies are small with few events, 20 we conducted a sensitivity analysis using pooled estimates calculated with a fixed‐effects model, assuming that we are estimating a weighted average of effects across the populations. 25 In line with the guidelines, 20 the Peto 1‐step odds ratio method was used for outcomes with event rates <1% (referred to as Peto OR), while the Mantel–Haenszel method was applied for the others. To account for different durations of follow‐up among trials, another sensitivity analysis was performed using the incident rate of outcomes per person‐years to obtain the incident rate ratios of SGLT2is relative to control. Person‐years of follow‐up were calculated by multiplying the sample size with the average (mean/median) follow‐up duration.

To account for the different timings of SGLT2i initiation, 2 sensitivity analyses were conducted. The first analysis evaluated the efficacy and safety outcomes only in patients whose SGLT2i was initiated before hospital discharge. Specifically, the SOLOIST‐WHF (A Randomized, Double‐Blind, Placebo‐Controlled, Parallel‐Group, Multicenter Study to Evaluate the Effects of Sotagliflozin on Clinical Outcomes in Hemodynamically Stable Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Post Worsening Heart Failure) trial 11 included patients for whom the first dose of sotagliflozin or placebo was administered within 3 days after discharge in 51.2% of the cohort. Thus, the sensitivity analysis was conducted by retaining only patients whose treatment was initiated before discharge, as reported later in a post hoc analysis. 26 A fourth sensitivity analysis included only the 5 RCTs in which the introduction of an SGLT2i was specifically carried out within the first 24 hours, thereby excluding SOLOIST‐WHF 11 and EMPULSE (Empagliflozin in Patients Hospitalized for Acute Heart Failure). 12
The last sensitivity analysis was performed after excluding the 2 open‐label RCTs included (Charaya et al 13 and DICTATE‐AHF [Efficacy and Safety of Dapagliflozin in Acute Heart Failure] 16 ).
Given the concerns about the efficacy of SGLT2is based on diabetic status, 27 we further conducted a meta‐regression analysis to assess the effect of diabetes on efficacy and safety outcomes.

sec.title: Study Selection
sec.p: From 11 491 references retrieved by searching relevant online databases, 30 RCTs were selected for full‐text assessment of inclusion criteria on the basis of title and abstract screening. Finally, we included 7 RCTs that randomized a total of 2320 patients followed for a weighted mean of 175.4 (range, 30–276) days with 1114.9 patient‐years of follow‐up. Among them, 5 were double‐blinded (placebo‐controlled) while 2 were open label (controlled with AHF standard of care); 4 were multisite and 3 were single‐site. The main elements of the protocol and the characteristics of the studied populations are presented in Tables 1 and 2. A flowchart of literature retrieval and reasons for article exclusion are shown in Figure 1.

sec.title: Risk of Bias
sec.p: Overall, all studies were categorized as “low” risk of bias according to the 5 fields in the Risk of Bias 2 tool (Figure 2). In the study by Charaya et al, 13 “some concerns” about bias due to deviations from intended interventions were identified, given that the investigator was not blinded (open‐label trial). The SOLOIST‐WHF 11 trial was reported as having “some concerns” due to a change in the primary end point during the course of the trial that may introduce bias in the selection of the reported result.

sec.title: Efficacy Outcomes
sec.p: Early use of SGLT2is compared with usual medical therapy was associated with a significant reduction in all‐cause death (OR, 0.71 [95% CI, 0.55–0.92; I 2=0%; τ2=0.0141; 95% PI, 0.55–0.98]) and HF rehospitalizations (OR, 0.73 [95% CI, 0.57–0.94], I 2=0%; τ2=0; 95% PI, 0.58–0.93]). There was no evidence of a difference for the composite outcome of cardiovascular death or HF events (OR, 0.52 [95% CI, 0.13–2.13; I 2=5%; τ2=0.0019]), although the estimated OR had a wide CI, as the calculation was based on only 2 studies (Figure 3A).

sec.title: Safety Outcomes
sec.p: We detected no statistically significant differences between SGLT2is and control arms for AKI (OR, 1.05 [95% CI, 0.51–2.19; I 2=50%; τ2=0.3105; 95% PI, 0.34–3.22]), hypoglycemia (OR, 1.25 [95% CI, 0.79–1.99; I 2=0%; τ2=0; 95% PI, 0.77–2.04]), hypotension (OR, 1.12 [95% CI 0.71–1.77; I 2=0%, τ2=0, 95% PI, 0.74–1.70]), ketoacidosis (OR, 0.69 [95% CI, 0.35–1.39; I 2=0%, τ2=0, 95% PI, 0.24–5.89]), and urinary tract infections (OR, 0.82 [95% CI, 0.59–1.12; I 2=0%; τ2=0; 95% PI, 0.54–1.23]). However, the 95% CIs were wide, encompassing the neutral effect, with a range of potential effects that span from benefit to harm (Figure 4A).

sec.title: Sensitivity Analyses
sec.p: The results derived from the fixed‐effects model (Figure S1) were generally consistent with those from the random‐effects model, demonstrating a significant association with a reduction in all‐cause death (OR, 0.73 [95% CI, 0.55–0.97; I 2=0%; τ2=0.0141]) and HF rehospitalizations (OR, 0.73 [95% CI, 0.58–0.93; I 2=0%; τ2=0]), along with an additional reduction in the risk of cardiovascular death or HF events (OR, 0.52 [95% CI, 0.42–0.64; I 2=5%; τ2=0.0019]). No significant differences were observed for any safety outcomes, including AKI (OR, 0.94 [95% CI, 0.68–1.31; I 2=50%; τ2=0.3105]), hypoglycemia (OR, 1.25 [95% CI, 0.78–2.02; I 2=0%; τ2=0]), hypotension (OR, 1.12 [95% CI, 0.74–1.68; I 2=0%; τ2=0]), ketoacidosis (Peto OR, 0.70 [95% CI, 0.21–2.28; I 2=0%; τ2=0]), or urinary tract infections (OR, 0.81 [95% CI, 0.54–1.21; I 2=0%; τ2=0]). Overall, both the random‐effects and fixed‐effects models yielded similar results, suggesting low heterogeneity between the studies.

Sensitivity analyses focusing on patients for whom an SGLT2i was initiated before discharge yielded consistent results, with a significant decrease in all‐cause death (OR, 0.52 [95% CI, 0.40–0.68; I 2=0%; τ2=0; 95% PI, 0.34–0.79]), although the rate of HF rehospitalizations (OR, 0.90 [95% CI, 0.56–1.43; I 2=0%; τ2=0; 95% PI, 0.57–1.42]) and cardiovascular death of HF events (OR, 0.56 [95% CI, 0.10–3.32; I 2=0%; τ2=0]) did not reach significance (Figure 3B). This analysis also showed no significant difference for all adverse events studied, including AKI (OR, 1.14 [95% CI, 0.42–3.09; I 2=60%; τ2=0.5260; 95% PI, 0.22–5.57]), hypoglycemia (OR, 0.93 [95% CI, 0.42–2.07; I 2=0%; τ2=0; 95% PI, 0.46–2.01]), hypotension (OR, 0.80 [95% CI, 0.37–1.75; I 2=0%; τ2=0; 95% PI, 0.39–1.66]), ketoacidosis (OR, 1.45 [95% CI, 0.06–37.52; I 2=0%; τ2=0; 95% PI, 0.24–5.89]), and urinary tract infections (OR, 0.87 [95% CI, 0.44–1.70; I 2=0%; τ2=0.0348; 95% PI, 0.54–1.41]), although the 95% CIs were again relatively wide due to the low number of observed events (Figure 4B). Both sensitivity analyses, focusing on treatment initiation within the first 24 hours, and after exclusion of open‐label RCTs (342 patients), did not reach statistical significance for any of the efficacy or safety outcomes (Figures S2 and S3). Nonetheless, the overall analysis including the duration of follow‐up, revealed results similar to those of the main analysis, with an improvement in all‐cause death, the rate of cardiovascular death or HF events, and the number of HF rehospitalizations (Figure S4). Meta‐regression analysis indicated no significant modification of efficacy or safety outcomes based on diabetic status, although the estimated coefficients had wide CIs due to the small number of included studies (Table S3).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: We present here the largest meta‐analysis of RCTs assessing efficacy and safety of early initiation of SGLT2is in 2320 patients hospitalized for AHF, regardless of LVEF or diabetic status. Hence, we provide evidence that, in settings of AHF (1) early use of SGLT2is is associated with a reduction in all‐cause death and HF rehospitalizations, and (2) initiation before discharge showed an even greater improvement in survival. These results advocate for the possible initiation of SGLT2is as soon as possible in patients with AHF according to inclusion/exclusion criteria used in the studies.

While both recent American and European HF consensus 1 , 6 , 7 , 28 clearly reaffirmed the imperative need to implement a 4‐drug therapy (GDMT) as soon as possible (SGLT2i, β blockers, angiotensin‐converting‐enzyme inhibitors/angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist), numerous studies identified critical gaps in the speed of their introduction, highlighting widespread therapeutic inertia. 29 , 30 A rapid uptitration of GDMT to the maximum tolerated dose is also a key point in both the American and European guidelines. 7 Yet, failure to initiate GDMT at discharge from an HF hospitalization is associated with a substantial risk that this therapy will never be initiated during subsequent follow‐ups or will be started with significant delay and an increase in mortality. 28 , 31 , 32 Conversely, improved survival is favored by and proportional to the number of GDMTs that can be introduced. 33 , 34 Some consensuses advocate for the introduction of the 4 pillars at least at a small dose, rather than prioritizing only 1 family, but the level of evidence remains poor. 35 The 2022 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association/Heart Failure Society of America guidelines also emphasize the recommendation that in patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction requiring hospitalization, preexisting GDMT should be maintained whenever possible. 7 They further highlight that the cornerstone of AHF management is the effectiveness of the decongestion strategy, recommending the addition of a second diuretic alongside loop diuretics when diuresis is inadequate to relieve symptoms. This approach could potentially include the use of SGLT2is. Whether in acute or chronic settings, it is often the fear of side effects (AKI, hypotension, ketoacidosis) that makes physicians reluctant to introduce and uptitrate GDMT, in both American and European reports. Our meta‐analysis demonstrates that, on the contrary, the introduction of SGLT2is before discharge can be performed safely, without increasing the risk of adverse events, while reducing all‐cause death by 46%, compared with 26% in the overall cohort, also including patients with introduction within 3 days after discharge. Therefore, their widespread and rapid use represents a significant opportunity to reduce post‐AHF death, which remains unacceptably high.

Previous smaller meta‐analyses, 36 , 37 which included only 3 RCTs, failed to show an improvement in mortality rate, although they did confirm progress in terms of HF events (eg, HF rehospitalizations or urgent visits) and self‐reported patient outcomes such as the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Total Symptom Score. There was also a slight nuance regarding the precise timing of SGLT2i initiation, particularly due to the inclusion of the SOLOIST trial, 11 where the treatment could be introduced either before discharge or within 3 days after discharge. The entirety of these favorable data supporting the early introduction of SGLT2is represents an opportunity to tackle therapeutic inertia in HF, where a large majority of patients are treated suboptimally, 17 even after an AHF episode.

The understanding of the mechanisms underlying the reduction in death and rehospitalizations with SGLT2is remains incomplete. Numerous studies conducted on both chronic and acute HF have revealed conflicting results regarding their renal effects, such as urinary volume, urinary sodium excretion, body weight change, and natriuretic peptides. 38 Besides these indices related to decongestion, SGLT2is are consistently associated with significant improvements in self‐reported outcomes, particularly through the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire score, 39 , 40 , 41 suggesting a beneficial effect on the cellular metabolism of cardiomyocytes, possibly not necessarily linked to the diuretic effect. They could have a more positive impact as the patients are sicker. 42 Interestingly, it has been shown that SGLT2is can produce cardioprotective effects in isolated cardiomyocytes (without expression of SGLT2) and in animal models in which SGLT2 expression has been suppressed. 43 , 44 Thus, further detailed studies are warranted to understand the true mechanisms of action of SGLT2is that lead to improved cardiac outcomes.

sec.title: Limitations and Future Directions
sec.p: There are several limitations to these meta‐analyses that should be noted. First, the duration of the intervention and the follow‐up were variable across all trials, although the validation of results on the efficacy and safety outcomes after standardizing the results as incident rate ratios helps to mitigate the impact of this bias. Due to the small number of included RCTs, detecting heterogeneity of effects was difficult, and measures of heterogeneity may be unreliable. Unfortunately, a significant portion of the analyses concerning the safety outcomes studied here is limited by the low number of observed events, resulting in wide CIs that encompass the neutral effect and a range of potential effects spanning from benefit to harm. Indeed, SGLT2is have already been distinguished by their relatively low rate of adverse events, particularly for ketoacidosis, which likely leads to a lack of power to detect significant differences in previous RCTs. 45 Nonetheless, further large‐scale pharmacovigilance real‐world studies could help formally clarify this aspect in the specific subpopulation of patients with AHF. Similarly, the results from the meta‐regression regarding the impact of diabetes status may also have been influenced by the small number of available RCTs. Given the lack of power previously described in RCTs evaluating the safety of SGLT2is, the gradual accumulation of future observational pharmacovigilance data will help clarify this point. Of note, the statistically significant results concerning all‐cause death and HF rehospitalizations were characterized by low heterogeneity between the studies, whether including exclusively diabetic patients or others.

Moreover, the sensitivity analyses conducted after excluding open‐label trials did not confirm the improvement in mortality rates and HF hospitalizations. Yet the risk of information bias does not appear to be substantial given the use of objective outcomes (all‐cause death, hospitalization) and standardized definitions. This difference may not be explained by a publication bias, since no other RCTs, even unpublished ones, were found on ClinicalTrials.gov, suggesting rather a probable lack of power following the exclusion of these patients. Additionally, some definitions of adverse events were inconsistent across trials, especially for AKI, with some studies using a definition based on a decrease in estimated glomerular filtration rate below a certain threshold, 9 , 10 , 11 while others used a threshold increase in creatinine. 14 , 15 Although no RCT specified inclusion restrictions on the basis of LVEF values, all RCTs primarily included patients with reduced or mildly reduced mean/median LVEF, limiting the strict applicability to patients with preserved LVEF, on whom further studies could focus.

Given the absence of available data in the majority of the included RCTs, we were unable to reliably describe certain clinically relevant outcomes, notably HF events, which encompass urgent visits and unplanned hospitalizations for acute HF, better representing worsening HF. Similarly, almost all the included RCTs (except SOLOIST‐WHF) considered HF rehospitalizations in a time‐to‐first‐event analysis. However, it might also be valuable to study the influence of SGLT2is on the total number of rehospitalizations, which is also an impactful perspective. Furthermore, all included RCTs excluded patients with chronic kidney disease with an estimated glomerular filtration rate <20–30 mL/min, so the results cannot be generalized to the population with severe renal insufficiency. Further studies could focus on these particular settings given the promising results of SGLT2is in AHF. Similarly, 5 of the 7 included RCTs (EMPA‐RESPONSE‐AHF [Empagliflozin in Patients Hospitalized for Acute Heart Failure], EMPULSE, Charaya et al, DAPA‐RESPONSE‐AHF [Effect of Adjuvant Dapagliflozin on Improving the Treatment of Congestion in Patients With Acute Heart Failure]) excluded patients with cardiogenic shock, and we therefore do not have specific data to draw conclusions for this specific issue. Of note, the EMPASHOCK (Effect at 3 Months of Early Empagliflozin Initiation in Cardiogenic Shock Patients on Mortality, Rehospitalization, Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction and Renal Function; NCT05879276) trial, which plans to assess efficacy and safety outcomes at 3 months for the use of empagliflozin in cardiogenic shock, will provide valuable insights. Eventually, our study included only molecules already tested in AHF settings (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and sotagliflozin). Future studies may also include other SGLT2is, such as canagliflozin or ertugliflozin.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Early introduction of SGLT2is in patients hospitalized for AHF improves all‐cause death and rehospitalization rates, can be performed before discharge, and should be offered to most patients with AHF.
